Did the Number of Complaints to the City Change in Different Neighborhoods After the Pandemic?

STA 9750 Individual Report, Team Focused (SQ4)

Author

Francisco Leon

Published

October 18, 2026

1. Introduction

Our team’s overarching question is: Did the COVID-19 pandemic change what New Yorkers want in a neighborhood? Each team member looks at one part of this question. My specific question (SQ4) is: Did the number of complaints to the city change in different neighborhoods after the pandemic?

Complaints to the city are a good way to see the daily quality of life in a neighborhood. People call 311 when there is too much noise, when the heat does not work, when the street is dirty, or when a car blocks their driveway. If complaints went up a lot in some neighborhoods and down in others, this can show where living conditions got worse or better after the pandemic. This connects to the work of my teammates, who look at prices, affordability, schools and crime in the same neighborhoods.

Following the team agreement, I compare two periods:

  • Pre-pandemic: 2018 and 2019
  • Post-pandemic: 2022 and 2023

I leave out 2020 and 2021 because they were the years of the pandemic itself, when the data was very unusual. The unit of analysis is the community district (59 in NYC), which is the same unit the rest of the team uses. Following the professor’s feedback, I use complaints per 1,000 residents so that districts and boroughs with different populations can be compared fairly.

2. Data

I use three data sources:

  1. 311 Service Requests from 2010 to 2019 (NYC Open Data, dataset 76ig-c548). It has about 22.6 million rows, one row per complaint.
  2. 311 Service Requests from 2020 to Present (NYC Open Data, dataset erm2-nwe9). Same format, updated daily.
  3. Population by community district (population_by_cd.csv), a file prepared by our team with 2020 Census population for each of the 59 community districts (NYC Department of City Planning). For borough totals I use the 2020 Census numbers published by the Department of City Planning.

The 311 data is available through the NYC Open Data API (Socrata) in CSV format. Each complaint has a date (created_date), a complaint type (complaint_type) and a community board (community_board), among other columns. The community board comes as text, for example "07 MANHATTAN", meaning district 7 inside the borough of Manhattan.

library(tidyverse)

3. Data Acquisition

The two 311 datasets are too big to download in full. Instead, I asked the API to count the complaints for me, grouped by community board and complaint type, so I only download the counts and not every complaint.

My first try asked the server for several years at once, and it never answered. The solution was a for loop that asks for one month at a time. Each month is a small query that the server can answer in a few seconds. The loop chooses the right dataset depending on the year, reads the result with read_csv(), and adds a column with the month. At the end, bind_rows() joins all the months into one table, and the result is saved as a CSV file. The if (!file.exists(...)) part means the download only runs the first time; after that, the code reads the saved file.

During the download, the connection to the server was cut twice. Because each month is saved in a list, I could continue from the last month that worked instead of starting again. The final table has 318,408 rows (48 months).

if (!file.exists("complaints_by_type_raw.csv")) {

  # First day of each month in 2018-2019 and 2022-2023 (48 months)
  type_months <- c(
    seq(as.Date("2018-01-01"), as.Date("2019-12-01"), by = "month"),
    seq(as.Date("2022-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-01"), by = "month")
  )

  type_list <- list()

  for (i in seq_along(type_months)) {

    start_date <- type_months[i]
    end_date   <- seq(start_date, by = "month", length.out = 2)[2]

    # 2018-2019 are in one dataset, 2022-2023 in another
    if (start_date < as.Date("2020-01-01")) {
      dataset_id <- "76ig-c548"
    } else {
      dataset_id <- "erm2-nwe9"
    }

    # Count complaints by community board and complaint type for this month
    my_url <- paste0(
      "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/", dataset_id, ".csv",
      "?$select=community_board,complaint_type,count(*) AS n",
      "&$where=created_date >= '", start_date, "T00:00:00'",
      " AND created_date < '", end_date, "T00:00:00'",
      "&$group=community_board,complaint_type&$limit=50000"
    )

    type_list[[i]] <- read_csv(URLencode(my_url), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
      mutate(month = start_date)
  }

  complaints_by_type_raw <- bind_rows(type_list)
  write_csv(complaints_by_type_raw, "complaints_by_type_raw.csv")
}

complaints_by_type_raw <- read_csv("complaints_by_type_raw.csv")

For the trend over time (Figure 1), I also downloaded total complaints per month and community board from January 2017 to September 2026, with the same month by month method (9,055 rows).

if (!file.exists("complaints_raw.csv")) {

  month_starts <- seq(as.Date("2017-01-01"), as.Date("2026-09-01"), by = "month")

  monthly_list <- list()

  for (i in seq_along(month_starts)) {

    start_date <- month_starts[i]
    end_date   <- seq(start_date, by = "month", length.out = 2)[2]

    if (start_date < as.Date("2020-01-01")) {
      dataset_id <- "76ig-c548"
    } else {
      dataset_id <- "erm2-nwe9"
    }

    my_url <- paste0(
      "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/", dataset_id, ".csv",
      "?$select=community_board,count(*) AS n",
      "&$where=created_date >= '", start_date, "T00:00:00'",
      " AND created_date < '", end_date, "T00:00:00'",
      "&$group=community_board&$limit=5000"
    )

    monthly_list[[i]] <- read_csv(URLencode(my_url), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
      mutate(month = start_date)
  }

  complaints_raw <- bind_rows(monthly_list)
  write_csv(complaints_raw, "complaints_raw.csv")
}

complaints_raw <- read_csv("complaints_raw.csv")

# Population by community district (file from the team, 2020 Census)
district_population <- read_csv("population_by_cd.csv") %>%
  select(boro_cd, population_2020)

4. Data Cleaning

I found three cleaning issues:

  1. Invalid community boards. Some complaints have values like "0 Unspecified", "Unspecified BRONX", missing values, or codes above 18 (for example "64 MANHATTAN" or "83 QUEENS"). Codes above 18 are Joint Interest Areas such as parks and airports, which have no residents. NYC has 59 real community districts, numbered inside each borough (Manhattan 1 to 12, Bronx 1 to 12, Brooklyn 1 to 18, Queens 1 to 14, Staten Island 1 to 3). I split the text into district number and borough with separate() and kept only district numbers 01 to 18. This removed 3.81% of the complaints (449,183 out of 11,785,984).
  2. Matching with the team. The team uses a code called boro_cd, where the first digit is the borough and the other two are the district (for example, 212 is Bronx 12). I created this code so my results can be joined with the rest of the team.
  3. Too many complaint types. The 311 data has more than 200 complaint types, and some names are written in different ways (for example “HEATING” and “HEAT/HOT WATER”). I grouped them into six groups with case_when() and str_detect(): Noise, Heat / Hot Water, Housing Conditions, Parking / Streets, Sanitation, and Other. I checked the biggest types left in “Other” and moved two that were in the wrong place (“Illegal Dumping” to Sanitation and “GENERAL” to Housing Conditions). The rest of “Other” includes water and sewer problems, trees, homeless assistance and food establishments.
valid_numbers <- c("01", "02", "03", "04", "05", "06", "07", "08", "09",
                   "10", "11", "12", "13", "14", "15", "16", "17", "18")

borough_codes <- tibble(
  borough      = c("MANHATTAN", "BRONX", "BROOKLYN", "QUEENS", "STATEN ISLAND"),
  borough_code = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
)

complaints_clean <- complaints_by_type_raw %>%
  separate(community_board, into = c("district_number", "borough"),
           sep = " ", extra = "merge", remove = FALSE) %>%
  filter(district_number %in% valid_numbers) %>%
  left_join(borough_codes, by = "borough") %>%
  mutate(
    boro_cd    = borough_code * 100 + as.numeric(district_number),
    year       = year(month),
    period     = if_else(year <= 2019, "Pre", "Post"),
    type_lower = str_to_lower(complaint_type),
    complaint_group = case_when(
      str_detect(type_lower, "noise") ~ "Noise",
      str_detect(type_lower, "heat|hot water") ~ "Heat / Hot Water",
      str_detect(type_lower, "plumbing|paint|plaster|unsanitary|water leak|door/window|electric|floor|appliance|general construction|mold|elevator") | type_lower == "general" ~ "Housing Conditions",
      str_detect(type_lower, "parking|driveway|street|sidewalk|traffic|vehicle|curb") ~ "Parking / Streets",
      str_detect(type_lower, "sanitation|dirty|garbage|litter|collection|rodent|graffiti|bulky|waste|recycling|dumping") ~ "Sanitation",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

# Checks

total_after  <- sum(complaints_clean$n)

5. Analysis

For each community district, I calculate the average number of complaints per year in each period (the total of the two years divided by 2). Then I calculate two measures of change:

  • Percent change: (Post - Pre) / Pre × 100
  • Rate change: (Post - Pre) / population × 1,000, which is the change in yearly complaints per 1,000 residents

These two columns, together with boro_cd, are saved in a CSV file for the team’s combined regression.

district_change_csv <- complaints_clean %>%
  group_by(boro_cd) %>%
  summarize(
    pre_per_year  = sum(n[period == "Pre"]) / 2,
    post_per_year = sum(n[period == "Post"]) / 2
  ) %>%
  left_join(district_population, by = "boro_cd") %>%
  mutate(
    complaint_pct_change  = round((post_per_year - pre_per_year) / pre_per_year * 100, 4),
    complaint_rate_change = round((post_per_year - pre_per_year) / population_2020 * 1000, 4)
  )

# Checks
nrow(district_change_csv)                         # 59
[1] 59
sum(is.na(district_change_csv$population_2020))   # 0
[1] 0
sum(district_change_csv$complaint_pct_change > 0) # districts that went up
[1] 52
district_change_csv %>%
  select(boro_cd, complaint_pct_change, complaint_rate_change) %>%
  write_csv("sq4_311_complaint_change.csv")

I also calculate the rate per 1,000 residents for each complaint group, district and period. This is used in Figures 3 and 4.

group_order <- c("Noise", "Heat / Hot Water", "Housing Conditions",
                 "Parking / Streets", "Sanitation", "Other")

group_rates <- complaints_clean %>%
  group_by(boro_cd, community_board, period, complaint_group) %>%
  summarize(complaints_per_year = sum(n) / 2, .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(district_population, by = "boro_cd") %>%
  mutate(
    rate_per_1000   = complaints_per_year / population_2020 * 1000,
    period          = factor(period, levels = c("Pre", "Post")),
    complaint_group = factor(complaint_group, levels = group_order)
  )

6. Results

Figure 1: Complaints per 1,000 residents by borough over time

borough_population <- tibble(
  borough    = c("BRONX", "BROOKLYN", "MANHATTAN", "QUEENS", "STATEN ISLAND"),
  population = c(1472654, 2736074, 1694251, 2405464, 495747)
)

monthly_rate <- complaints_raw %>%
  separate(community_board, into = c("district_number", "borough"),
           sep = " ", extra = "merge", remove = FALSE) %>%
  filter(district_number %in% valid_numbers, year(month) >= 2018) %>%
  group_by(month, borough) %>%
  summarize(total_complaints = sum(n), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(borough_population, by = "borough") %>%
  mutate(complaints_per_1000 = total_complaints / population * 1000)

ggplot(monthly_rate, aes(x = month, y = complaints_per_1000, color = borough)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title   = "Monthly 311 Complaints per 1,000 Residents by Borough, 2018-2026",
    x       = "Month",
    y       = "Complaints per 1,000 residents",
    color   = "Borough",
    caption = "Sources: NYC Open Data, 311 Service Requests; U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Before the pandemic, the five boroughs were very close, between about 18 and 30 complaints per 1,000 residents per month. In 2020 there is a short drop and then a big jump. After that, the boroughs separate. The Bronx becomes the highest, at about 40 to 50 complaints per 1,000 residents, with some peaks near 80. Staten Island stays the lowest. With raw counts, Brooklyn looked like the borough with the most complaints, so using rates per 1,000 residents changes the story, as the professor suggested.

Figure 2: Percent change in all 59 community districts

all_districts <- district_change_csv %>%
  left_join(complaints_clean %>% distinct(boro_cd, community_board, borough),
            by = "boro_cd") %>%
  mutate(borough = str_to_title(borough))

ggplot(all_districts,
       aes(x = complaint_pct_change,
           y = reorder(community_board, complaint_pct_change),
           fill = borough)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "Change in 311 Complaints in All 59 Community Districts",
    subtitle = "Percent change, Pre (2018-2019) vs Post (2022-2023)",
    x        = "Percent change (%)",
    y        = NULL,
    fill     = "Borough",
    caption  = "Source: NYC Open Data, 311 Service Requests"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))

Complaints went up in 52 of the 59 districts and went down in only 7. The biggest increase is Bronx 12 (Wakefield, Williamsbridge) with 123%, more than double any other district. Next are Manhattan 7 (Upper West Side), Bronx 8 (Riverdale, Kingsbridge), Manhattan 10 (Central Harlem) and Brooklyn 2 (Downtown Brooklyn, Fort Greene), all with increases of about 53% to 57%. Seven of the 10 districts with the biggest increase are in the Bronx. The districts where complaints went down are all three Staten Island districts, eastern Queens (Queens 11 and 13) and southern Brooklyn (Brooklyn 10 and 18). The biggest decrease is Staten Island 1, with about -15%.

Figure 3: Top 10 districts by complaint group

top_10_cd <- district_change_csv %>%
  slice_max(complaint_pct_change, n = 10) %>%
  pull(boro_cd)

group_rates %>%
  filter(boro_cd %in% top_10_cd) %>%
  mutate(community_board = reorder(community_board, match(boro_cd, top_10_cd))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = period, y = rate_per_1000, fill = complaint_group)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ community_board, nrow = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Top 10 Districts with the Biggest Increase in 311 Complaints",
    subtitle = "Yearly complaints per 1,000 residents by group, Pre (2018-2019) vs Post (2022-2023)",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Complaints per 1,000 residents",
    fill     = "Complaint group",
    caption  = "Sources: NYC Open Data, 311 Service Requests; NYC DCP, 2020 Census population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

This figure answers why the top districts changed. In Bronx 12, almost all of the increase comes from noise. Noise complaints went from 40.2 to 353.0 per 1,000 residents per year, about 8.8 times higher. Total complaints went from 305.5 to 682.2 per 1,000 residents, an increase of 376.7, and noise explains 312.8 of that increase (83%). In the other Bronx districts of the top 10, the increase is more spread out, with clear growth in Housing Conditions and Heat / Hot Water. In Brooklyn 2 and Bronx 8, Parking / Streets complaints grew a lot.

group_rates %>%
  filter(boro_cd == 212) %>%
  select(period, complaint_group, rate_per_1000) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = rate_per_1000) %>%
  mutate(change = Post - Pre)

Figure 4: Bottom 10 districts by complaint group

bottom_10_cd <- district_change_csv %>%
  slice_min(complaint_pct_change, n = 10) %>%
  pull(boro_cd)

group_rates %>%
  filter(boro_cd %in% bottom_10_cd) %>%
  mutate(community_board = reorder(community_board, match(boro_cd, bottom_10_cd))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = period, y = rate_per_1000, fill = complaint_group)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ community_board, nrow = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Bottom 10 Districts with the Lowest Change in 311 Complaints",
    subtitle = "Yearly complaints per 1,000 residents by group, Pre (2018-2019) vs Post (2022-2023)",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Complaints per 1,000 residents",
    fill     = "Complaint group",
    caption  = "Sources: NYC Open Data, 311 Service Requests; NYC DCP, 2020 Census population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The bottom 10 districts look very different from the top 10. Their total complaints per 1,000 residents are lower, and Parking / Streets is the biggest group in most of them. Noise is small, especially in Staten Island. The clearest change is that Sanitation complaints went down in almost all of these districts.

7. Limitations

  1. Fixed population. I use 2020 Census population for both periods, so the rates per 1,000 residents are an approximation. The population of NYC went down after 2020 and then recovered.
  2. More complaints do not always mean worse conditions. An increase can also mean that more people use 311, not only that problems got worse.
  3. Fewer complaints do not always mean better conditions. Staten Island is the least populated and least dense borough, so it naturally reports fewer complaints, for example about noise.
  4. Removed records. 3.81% of the complaints had no valid community district and were removed.
  5. Grouping by hand. The six complaint groups are based on the words in each complaint type. Some types may not fit perfectly in one group. Also, 311 changed some complaint type names over time, so part of the drop in Sanitation could come from these changes and not from real improvements. I did not fully verify this.
  6. No direct link to moving. Complaints show where conditions may have changed, but they do not prove that people moved to or away from a neighborhood.

8. Conclusion

Yes, the number of complaints to the city changed after the pandemic, and the change was very different across neighborhoods. Complaints went up in 52 of the 59 community districts. The biggest increases were concentrated in the Bronx, led by Bronx 12, where complaints more than doubled because of a large increase in noise complaints. Other Bronx districts saw more housing and heat complaints. The only decreases were in Staten Island, eastern Queens and southern Brooklyn, which are farther from Manhattan and less dense.

For our overarching question, this suggests that after the pandemic, quality of life problems grew most in dense neighborhoods, especially in the Bronx, while lower density areas stayed stable or improved. If people wanted more space and quieter areas after the pandemic, these lower density neighborhoods may have become more attractive. This is only one piece of the answer. The sq4_311_complaint_change.csv file with boro_cd, complaint_pct_change and complaint_rate_change will be combined with my teammates’ results on prices, affordability, schools and crime to test if changes in complaints are related to the other changes in each neighborhood.
